-- remember when you first started singing?

I have been singing all my life, ever since I can remember. We sang at home in Houston, Texas, in church. And I'm 80 years old, so I've been singing 80 years back, I was in the church. I started off singing in the church.
When you were real little?
When I was real little. When I was seven years old (unintelligible). I was already going to Sunday school.
And you remember when you first started playing the piano?
Played piano all my life. (Unintelligible). My whole family is musical. My brother made me take my first music lesson (unintelligible). He gave me my first music lesson.
Do you remember how old you were?
I was about 8.
Eight. And how old was he at that time?
Well, he was married, (inaudible) he must have been up in the 20's because he was married.
Did your mother play any instruments?
No, my mother never played. I don't know where we picked this up at because mama didn't play and papa didn't either. I don't know where we got the music from.

I don't know where we got that music from because mama didn't play and neither sing, no more than in church.
So you got it in the church, you think?
I guess so.
Uh-huh.

And my mother had 13 children, eight girls and five boys, and I was the 11th child, born in the 11th month, on the first day. And Herschel, that was my big brother, he was the second child. And my mother's sister, my mother had a girlfriend who (unintelligible), my mother's girlfriend, she took very sick and before she died she told my mother, she said, "Fanny, I'm going to go, I'm going to die." She said, you take my children and raise them. And mama took those children and raised them and one of her boys took my brother's wife, he was 11 years old (unintelligible) my brother's wife, because he just wanted to get away from home. He didn't need no woman (unintelligible). And then she got the baby with my brother and my mother raised her (unintelligible). And she was raised up with my sister because mama nursed her (unintelligible).
She was the singer, Lucille?
Lucille. (Unintelligible). But she and my sister -- she is one of my nieces (unintelligible). She died and her daughter had three children (unintelligible). Then I had to take them.
When did she die?
Hemlock Erasable
Flocille
Lucille, she must have died -- '54 -- she must have died -- I wouldn't know. She must have went and died in about '45, somewhere around there. Because these children wasn't born.
What kind of voice would you describe Lucille's voice as?
Just like mine.
Just like yours.
The (unintelligible). I got her records.
You've got her records?
No, I ain't got it but I could -- I may have one, or two (unintelligible).
Is that so?
(Inaudible) because we used to play together.
Did you ever make a record together with Lucille?
Uh-huh, we did in Chicago.
You did in Chicago?
Uh-huh.
For Okeh?
Yeah, for O.K. (Unintelligible).
You and Lucille both singing?
Yeah.
Together?
No, not together, separate. (Unintelligible). I song was "Deep Water Blues."
How is that, again?
"Deep Water Blues."
Oh, "Deep Water Blues."
Yeah, yeah. After she (unintelligible) well, I've been thinking about taking it myself, "Deep Water Blues."
Did she play the piano?
Yeah, she played beautiful. Played better than I did. Because I was more church than she was. She wasn't churchy, like me.
She was more blues?
Yeah, she always was blues. She always was and I was church music. But we still remember, she was always -- my mom made us go to church (unintelligible). But I was always was churchy.
Did you go to school in Texas?

Yeah. And she did too. Went to Dunbar as for as School. I went -- I got moved to 10th grade (unintelligible). It was just in high school (unintelligible) in the Fourth Ward in Houston, Texas. We went to 7th grade in the Second ward (?) and I went to primary (unintelligible) Dunbar School (unintelligible). We went to Grace Lawrence, first, Kindergarten. Kindergarten (unintelligible) and first grade to seventh, wanted to move
me (unintelligible) to the school.
Did you have music in the schools?
Yeah, we had concerts. Used to take me every Friday, to different schools, and sing for them.
Always was a singer. We always were taken to a school to sing. We'd sing for the schools. All we would do.
What were you singing?
The teacher would learn me a song to sing.
Oh, yeah.

(Unintelligible) "So long," (unintelligible) "that means goodby, to you." (Singing, words unintelligible). My teacher learned me that (unintelligible). And learned (unintelligible). And my cousin told me, said, will you sing your song? "Sippie," (unintelligible).
What was that, about 1910, huh?
About '10.
Uh-huh. Yessuh.
That's very interesting. Were you the only one they took around to sing in the schools?
I'm the only girl, I'm the only girl they took around. I was in third grade then. Now, they took take with me, (unintelligible) and he used to (unintelligible). We were the only two (unintelligible).
What were you doing, singing?
Singing. We used to have a kind of song (unintelligible) and I remember the song we'd sing, (unintelligible).
And when you left school what did you do?

My momma died. That's how come I leavel school, (unintelligible) my momma died, you know. And see my brother, he was married and he (unintelligible). Every 16th, they used to pay just all once a month, in Houston then, at that time. But now the they wanted (unintelligible) they pay twice a month now. But at home you were paid once a month, and it was the 16th. My And I can't wait brother would come in and bring his money home. (unintelligible) my brother would always give my mother a little piece of change, you know, and (unintelligible) keep the baby until I tell was coming back. I tell him never come back. So mama told brother, said (unintelligible) so he said, "Mama, hadn't you better take the baby because I can't take care of a baby." (Unintelligible). So she said, (unintelligible). When she it was did come back in about 10 years or more.
That's hard times.
Uh-huh. (Unintelligible), He went back to her and she (unintelligible), Got another baby. And my brother said he didn't believe (unintelligible).
Was your father home when your mother died?
No, my father died first.
He died first?
Uh-huh.
What did he do? What kind of work did he do?
S.P. Worked in shops.
Butcher shop?
No, S.P. Shop.
S. P. Shop?
Makes engines, trains.
Oh, trains.
Made trains. See, that's what my brother did until he started writing music.
Your brother George?
Uh-huh. If he (unintelligible) he never would have started writing music if (unintelligible). He wrote music to pacify his mind. And I was so in love with my brother.
Why was it -- his heart was broken when your mother died, is that --
When his wife went off and left him.
Oh, when his wife went off and left him. And that's when he started writing music. I see.
(Inaudible) (singing). "Why from me did you part? Dear, you surely broke my heart (inaudible). I am lonely and blue, I don't know what to do (unintelligible).

Why from me did you roam? Did you know I won't be home? Tell me dear, when are you coming back? (Unintelligible). Come back to me, please, come back home. Until you find you want to roam. You know, dear, I love you so. Take your time and listen to me, hon, come back home. Please come back home. Tell me that you will never roam. If you have a heart, my dear, then come back home again, dear, to your baby. Come back home, again, dear." That's the whole song.
A beautiful song.
And I have made (unintelligible).
It's beautiful.
Ain't it pretty.
Yeah, sure is.

(Inaudible) I should have recorded it a long time ago, made a record then, but I didn't want my brother to think about it, until she -- let him forget her. Because she sure (unintelligible). So sad. My mother went down to see my brother and he had a whole five gallon can of kerosene (unintelligible).
Oh, my.
He said. (Unintelligible)
(Recording interruption.)
How long after that --
(Recording interruption.)
(Unintelligible) after momma died, my older brother, George Thomas, he -- and Mr. Peeler was my
manager then, from New York City.
Was George already in Chicago?
Oh, yeah. And (unintelligible). We called him Buddy, you know.
Your brother you called Buddy?
Yeah.
George you called Buddy?

Uh-huh. So she asked Buddy, do you have any blues? See, the world was going crazy about blues singing. And so my brother stammered a lot, you know. And he said, I got a sister who's coming from Texas. She got something maybe (inaudible). And I played (unintelligible) with them wierd names (unintelligible) I had to play some blues, and I didn't know how to name them but my brother did. So my brother taught me how to make a story, make a song sound like a story. And then after I played a song, (unintelligible) I played one song, it was the same as Thomas but different -- a little different. So he told my brother, that's what we want. Talk with her, she's got exactly what we want. Supper you that's it. Said, have her down in the Loop. The same -- he said 2:00 o'clock, and he give Brother a contract right there. (Unintelligible) got a job. (Unintelligible) I would play and he wrote it. (Unintelligible) Make sense, you know, make a story. (Unintelligible)
So we named that one song, then we had the other side,
that's when I made the "Showgirl Blues."
Oh, you did that, the "Country Blues," first?
No, it's something (unintelligible) in the writing.
Yeah, uh-huh.
Now, when I wrote the song, I did "Shortly George" and "Caledonia" (unintelligible).
"Caledonia?"
Yeah. (Humming). That's some real, great hit. (Singing).
But now my brother couldn't play that. My little brother could play that. (Unintelligible).
(Piano)
(Unintelligible).
Yes.
So I played (unintelligible).
Ms. Wallace, that nice style that you had that your brother George took you to show the Okeh people, would you say anybody influenced you? How did you learn that style?
Which style?
The way you sang, you know, the way you sang the blues. The way you sang. Would you say you learned that from the church?
I learned that from hearing blues
No, (unintelligible) I got that from my own blues. (Unintelligible) I guess I really was a blues singer (unintelligible).
Well, did you ever hear any blues singers before you started singing blues?
(Unintelligible). I'd be sitting on the front porch, I would hear (unintelligible) victrola, and used to play our records (unintelligible) if I sat on my porch I could hear it.
What kind of records did he play that you heard?
(Unintelligible).
Oh, Mamie Smith?
Mamie Smith.
Uh-huh.
And Bess Smith wasn't on with her then.
No, not yet.
All it was was Mamie Smith.
Yeah. So you heard those Mamie Smith records.
I used to get all Mamie Smith records.
Uh-huh.
(Unintelligible). I used to listen to every one of her songs.
So you heard those and --
I learned by hearing her songs.
That's very interesting. But of course, your style was very different than Mamie Smith's. You used your own style
(Unintelligible) that was the main thing he told me back there (unintelligible) he said, you sing just like Bessie Smith.
You think so?
That's what he told me. I don't know, I think I sing like myself.
I do, too. I think you sing like yourself.
Yeah, but everybody told me I sing like Bessie Smith.

You know, I heard and read that when a record of yours would come out in Chicago, people would stand in line at Clarence William's Store. That's what I heard, stand in long lines, a block long, to get a new record by Sippie Wallace.

I know. I know in Dallas, Texas some people would stand in line. I was (unintelligible) tell me that for three or two weeks, that people would stay out there two weeks (unintelligible). A line as long as you could see.
How did that make you feel as a young girl?
I didn't know everybody was out there. I didn't know they was out there.
Oh, you didn't know that?
I didn't know that. (Unintelligible).
Did you know about it in Chicago?
No, I didn't know.
That they stood in line at Clarence William's Store?

No, I never know. I heard (unintelligible) at Louisiana-Alley last year, they had (unintelligible) my daughter, she go to college, and she bought one of those books and she pulled a leaf out, they say I was dead. Said I died in '52.
Oh, that's terrible.

Said I was dead. (Unintelligible). I said, no, I wouldn't do that, maybe she got the wrong understanding, you know. It might be (unintelligible). So when I went to (unintelligible). But why they have me, say I died in '52. (Unintelligible).
Well, you sure look alive to me. And you certainly very lively.
Well then, I noticed your first records, or some of your records were Sipple Thomas.

Well, that's my maiden name. See, I'll tell you about that, how that was done. See, I don't know for sure but this is what I believe, my manager and the people had an argument. And he then left and went to the

Colonial people (unintelligible). He left the Okeh and came over to (unintelligible). So when he called me to Richard, (unintelligible). And they had my records, Sippie Thomas. So he made my name Sippie Thomas over there. So while (unintelligible) he said the records, Sippie Wallace and Sippie Thomas was the same people. He said, how'd you have two names? I said, I don't know. Somebody sold me, unbeknownst to myself.
(Recording interruption.)
Now, these Victor labels, Ms. Wallace, that I've got listed as Sippie Thomas --
Yeah.

"Go Down," "Sunshine Blues," that was unissued. "But You're Going to Need My Help," "A Mighty Tight Woman," those were issued by Victor under the name Sippie Thomas. And "Ain't Nobody Home but Me." They cut that but didn't issue it.
"Anybody but Me"?
Yeah.

You know how they -- they put it out but my husband was living during the time and he woke up one day and they put some bluebird singing on the back of there, and my husband stopped that record, "Ain't Nobody Home but Me." He stopped it. He heard singing, he said, "Sip, that's you a record that had some bluebird singing but they got -- (unintelligible)."
So was that you?
That was me.
They called you Sippie Thomas, here on these Victors? Was that you singing on those?
Yeah, that was me. Because Matt told me.
Yeah, with Johnny Dodds, with Kid Ory -- do you remember if Kid Ory was on those?
No, I don't remember.
But you say you never got any money for those?
Not a dime (unintelligible).
Not a dime. How about that. That was February, 1929?
Uh-huh.
How did they get those sides?
I'll be darned if I know.
Did you record those for Victor?
I recorded for Victor, let's see, I had to record for Victor. Mr. Peeler took me over. I don't know how I got over to Victor but I (unintelligible).
Yeah. Well, didn't Victor pay you?
I don't remember receiving no money from Victor. I don't remember receiving one dime from Victor.
My goodness. Was that Mr. Pierce still your agent then, at that time?

No, after -- see, around then, Mr. told me that Mr. Pierce wasn't up there no more. But he carried me over -- I got this contract from the Victor people, but my brother wouldn't let me (unintelligible).
Well, at that time, that was 1929, you were very popular then.
I know. See, I played lots of music, see. See, I stayed long there, nobody know where I was. And they kept (unintelligible).
Where were you?
I was in Chicago.
Well, why were people asking about you? Weren't you around singing?
I didn't know they wanted [me]. were.
You didn't know they wanted you?
Mr. Pierce -- it was Mr. Pierce kept all the mail that was mailed to me. I didn't get it. Mr. Pierce robbed me of that.
What were you doing in Chicago then?
Living with my brother.
With your brother?
Uh-huh (unintelligible).
But you weren't singing in the clubs?
Yeah, I was singing.
You were singing in the clubs?
Oh, no, I wasn't singing in clubs then.
No?
Uh-uh.
When did you start singing in the clubs?
After I come back from Detroit.
Oh, you didn't sing in the clubs in Chicago?
Uh-uh,
No?
Uh-uh,
Oh, I see. Why not?

I was too young, I was too young in those days, I didn't know how to do -- I didn't know (unintelligible). I was too young to go in them clubs (unintelligible). They wouldn't let me go in places. After it got to be (unintelligible), I knew a lot of people here. I knew a lot of girls here, (Unintelligible). I used to play the (unintelligible). (Laughter.)
And all they wanted to know, could you play the piano and sing? And Bess (?) would get to the piano and play and I would sing. And they let us in there. (Unintelligible).
Do you remember when that was?
Yeah, I don't know what year it was but I remember.
That was when you were living in New York?
I was living in New York.
Who were you living with in New York then?
Buddy.
With Buddy.
Oh, no, I was staying around the corner, 11th Avenue and 144th Street.
Who were you living with, your brother?
Had a room.
Roomed by yourself?
Me and Herschel.
You and Herschel.
My little brother.
Uh-huh. Your little brother. And Fats would come by?
Yeah, he always come by there. (Unintelligible) have a good time. He'd take me, going to go out, to (Unintelligible) whenever he was
Well, did you go to some of those rent parties?

I went to all of them. (Unintelligible). I'd go to all of them. And this girl, who I was staying with, we had so much (Unintelligible) there at the house, I didn't have to go (Unintelligible) and we played bridge or gin rummy, you know. We played (Unintelligible) drink beer. We had that at the house, you know, because my music then, the more whiskey and beer and stuff (Unintelligible) with the song, you know.
Because everytime I'd get ready to go and do a record, I always -- little brothers give me a shot before I go, make me sing with vim, you know.
Give you a shot of whiskey before you sang on a record?
(Unintelligible).
Oh, uh-huh. But you didn't work in any of the clubs in New York?
No.
No. Well, when you were in Chicago, making all those records, didn't you work at the Dreamland Cafe, or Royal Garden Cafe?
Uh-uh. Wouldn't let me do it.
Who wouldn't let you do that?
My husband wouldn't.
Oh, your husband. I see.

I wasn't -- too young, I wouldn't know how to get around (unintelligible). And I didn't know anybody and I dasn't go by myself, you know. Because I had a girlfriend -- or even a man pair, you know. My husband would go (unintelligible) and all them around there. But that would be him going. (Unintelligible). So sometime when there would be a brawl, she wouldn't go out of the room.
Well, you didn't see Lil and Louis, then, playing at the Dreamland?
Oh, no. Never.
Are you never saw King Oliver?
Oh, yeah, he was my --
Did you see King Oliver?
Yeah, he was my -- he used to play with me all the time. (Unintelligible).
So King Oliver you saw.
Yeah.
Was that after Louis and Lil left him?
No, that was during the time, you know.
When Lil and Louis were playing with King Oliver?

Yeah, see (unintelligible). They always give me whatever I wanted to play with me. I wanted to take Basie, Louis Armstrong, and I would keep my little brother, Herschel. And Richard with trombone. I even stopped having Buddy (unintelligible) with the band because he would play too loud.
Who played too loud?
Buddy Christian, with the band.
Oh, Buddy Christian.
Uh-huh.
Who did you have on drums? Did you have drums?
No.
Didn't have drums. Now, you picked them.
Let's see now, when you had Louie in 1924, he was playing with Fletcher Henderson, and that was in New York. Do you remember that?
Seems like I remember.
That was Clarence William's then band,
Clarence Williams Blues Five.
Yeah.
Do you remember that?
Yeah, I sang with him a long time, too.
Yeah.

See, it was a long time before I got Herschel. See, I had to get Herschel -- I had to break Herschel in. See, I didn't have Herschel, my little brother Herschel, to play with me (unintelligible). I had a little girl named Lil Creole. Her name was Creole, you know, and she wouldn't play with me because I wouldn't put her name on the record. See, I could tell somebody (unintelligible).
Well now, you played in 1924 with Clarence Williams?
Uh-huh.
And those records you made in New York? Right?
Uh-huh.
Do you remember when Sidney Bechet played with you?
Yeah, I remember (unintelligible). I liked Bechet playing. I love his (unintelligible). I like a sax.
You like a sax?
Yeah.
You like that voice?
I like the voice.
The tunes you did with Bechet and Clarence Williams and Buddy Christian on the banjo, 'I'm So Glad I'm Brown Skinned,'
Yeah.
Do you remember that?
Yeah (unintelligible).
Yeah?
(Unintelligible) he sent me about six records.
Who sent them to you?
Clarence Williams' son, I think.
Oh, yeah? That was nice of him.
That one, he say, 'Sippie,' he say, 'We got some of your records, I thought maybe you'd want to have.'
That was very good.
(Unintelligible). "The Devil Done Blues,"
How about 'Off and On Blues', did you
get that one? Because Bechet was on that one, too.
Was he?
Yeah. Do you remember that?
Yeah, that made a big hit. That was one of the (unintelligible) said, Sippie, you got a real hit "Off and On Blues" on the way. He said (unintelligible). And I had forgot about it.
You forgot about it?
I had done forgot about it. So he made Bechet?
Yeah, Bechet was on that one with you.
I didn't know Bechet was on it. I got it.
You got it now? (Unintelligible).
(Unintelligible).
Did you write that song?
Uh-uh.
No?
(Unintelligible) and somebody sent them to the (unintelligible).
And did you pick the ones you wanted?
(End of side one, as recorded)
They ran me in there. The man (unintelligible). This was money to (unintelligible) like you owe
me some and wanted me to sing, and he would give me (unintelligible).
I see. The man who wrote the songs?
Uh-huh.
When you went to the O.K. office, is that it?
Uh-huh.
To record?
Uh-huh.
You would sing his songs?
Uh-huh.
Oh, so you saw the songs for the first time when you went to record? You didn't practice it? Did you practice it?
No, I didn't practice.
Did you read music? Did you know how to read music?
Not too good. But see, I sing music and I wasn't going to play it, no how. It was (unintelligible) played, he'd play and I'd sing it down the road and (unintelligible).
Now here, for example, in February 1925, Joe Oliver was playing for you, playing coronet, and your brother Herschel was playing the piano?
Uh-huh.
For "Mourning Dove Blues".
"Mourning Dove Blues." I made a big hit, too.
Yeah. "Devil Dance Blues", "Every Dog Has Its Day".
Uh-huh.
Now, you remember who wrote those songs?
No, I (unintelligible),
You wrote "Devil Dance Blues"?
Uh-huh.
Now, in a case like that, would somebody -- would another song writer put the money on for the song, either of those two, like "Every Dog has His Day" or "Mourning Dove Blues"?
See, you remember, "Every Dog Has His Day", I wrote that, too.
Oh, that's yours, yeah.
Yeah, I wrote that, too. (Unintelligible).
Right.
(Unintelligible).
Yeah. Did you ever learn to read music?
Yeah, I learned to read music.
Eventually?
Well, I know how to read music, but you read too much music you get (unintelligible) you can't read

harmony. You can't write harmony. So I puts all my music at home. And I know the scale, A, B, C, D, E, F, and G. But I studied harmony. Now, if you want to put me (unintelligible) play a song in F or A, do a song in G, that's G.
(Piano).

I know where I can play every key. Any key you can sing, I can change it around so I knows how to play every song in any key. Any song, if you can't sing in one key, I'll put it in your key. You know, so many people don't know what key you sing in. You can sing a song (unintelligible) but you don't know what key you're singing, you know. But I know my key. And (inaudible) teached me, always know your key. Know your key. Then you can tell, play me a song in G. Play me something in C, or play me a song in C, you know. And then you'll know (unintelligible). You know, what key to sing. (Unintelligible).

Ms. Wallace, in November 1926, around -- in 1926, I see that they say here that there was a Cicero Thomas who played the coronet. And somebody else wrote underneath it that you never knew somebody by that name.
I never,
I wonder why they made a mistake like that and put a name down like Cicero Thomas for coronet in those tunes. It was "I'm a Mighty Tight Woman" and --
I know, they told me (unintelligible)
about somebody singing "I'm a Mighty Tight Woman." He said, somebody's singing your tune.
Oh, it was somebody else singing, then?
He said, somebody's singing your tune. And somebody just recorded my tune (unintelligible).
This was in 1926 (unintelligible)?
No, this was what the man told me when I was (unintelligible).
Oh, I get it. Isn't that funny.
What they would do, they would take your music and there was nothing you could do about it. Nothing you could do about it.
And you never did know such a man?
No.
No way?
No. They take your music and go on singing it. Now I sing, but you know, sometimes (unintelligible).
(Piano)

Now, here's a song I like, I know somebody else wrote it, but the song fits me to a tee. See my man, my husband died, the story of it piqued me. I told people, I don't care what you've got (unintelligible).
(Singing).

"Told my friends, I didn't care, (unintelligible). "I laughed the day I saw you leave. I laughed the day I saw you leave, but after my laughter came tears. (Unintelligible). After my laughter came tears." (Unintelligible).
Very nice.
"After my Laughter Came Tears." Now, that song fits me to a tee. But I know somebody wrote it. If I tried to sing it and say I wrote it, I'd be put in jail. But the song's really my story.
It's beautiful.
I told the man, told my brothers, (unintelligible) after that man died, it liked to kill me. I'm just, you know, it's about the last two years (unintelligible).
Well, I lost plenty of men. I've lost plenty of men.
The men, the ones you lose?
Oh, it's a hard question. It's a hard question.
(Unintelligible). And I'd be getting in bed, and then after while I'd reach out and there'd be nothing but the pillows. And then you get the blues so bad. (Unintelligible).
Now, who are you talking about?
The man (unintelligible).
Your husband?
No, not my real husband. The man I had after my husband died.
Who was he? What was his name?
His name was Buddy. His name was Buddy, too (unintelligible).
I see.
(Unintelligible).
How long were you with him?
All my life (unintelligible).
Oh, you were with him long.
See, my husband died pretty soon after (unintelligible), but this man, ever since my husband been dead.
Oh, so you were with him a very long time?

segments.title: Opening of the Smithsonian interview, April 1979
segments.summary: Header and title page of the Smithsonian Jazz Oral History interview, cassette sides 1-2.

segments.title: First singing and piano lessons in Houston
segments.summary: Wallace has sung since childhood in church and played piano from about age eight, taught by her brother; her parents were not musical.

segments.title: Her mother's thirteen children and niece Hocile
segments.summary: She describes her large family, the children her mother raised, and her niece who sang and died in the 1940s.

segments.title: Niece Hocile's voice, a record together, church versus blues
segments.summary: Hocile sang just like her and recorded for Okeh in Chicago; Hocile played better piano and leaned toward blues while Sippie was church-minded.

segments.title: Schools in Houston and singing solos for other schools
segments.summary: She went to school in Houston's wards and was taken every Friday to sing for other schools, taught songs by her teacher.

segments.title: Leaving school when her mother died; her father's railroad shop work
segments.summary: She left school when her mother died, recalls a brother's marriage and money, and says her father died first and worked in the shops.

segments.title: Brother George starts writing music after his wife leaves
segments.summary: George, who had worked on trains, began writing music to ease his heartbreak; she sings the song and recalls him in despair.

segments.title: George in Chicago and the Okeh audition
segments.summary: Her brother George, called Buddy, tells the Okeh people about his sister from Texas; she plays and sings for them and is given a contract.

segments.title: Where her blues style came from; hearing Mamie Smith records
segments.summary: She says she got her blues from within and from Mamie Smith records heard from her porch; people told her she sounded like Bessie Smith.

segments.title: Crowds queuing for her records; a book reports her dead
segments.summary: Reitz says fans queued at Clarence Williams's store for her records; Wallace knew nothing of it and found a book listing her as dead in 1952.

segments.title: Sippie Thomas name and the Victor sides she was never paid for
segments.summary: Her records appeared as Sippie Thomas, her maiden name, after her manager changed companies; she recalls the 1929 Victor sides and never being paid.

segments.title: Mr. Pierce, the withheld mail and the missing years
segments.summary: Her manager Mr. Pierce kept her mail so she did not know the record companies wanted her; she was living with her brother in Chicago.

segments.title: Too young to sing in Chicago clubs
segments.summary: She was not singing in Chicago clubs because she was too young; she began after returning from Detroit and recalls getting in with a pianist friend.

segments.title: Living in New York with Herschel; rent parties and drinks before records
segments.summary: In New York she roomed with her little brother Herschel, Fats came by, she went to rent parties and was given a shot before recording.

segments.title: Not working Chicago clubs because of her husband; seeing King Oliver
segments.summary: Her husband would not let her work the Dreamland or Royal Garden; she never saw Lil and Louis there but did see King Oliver.

segments.title: Choosing sidemen; Clarence Williams and Lil Creole
segments.summary: She says she could pick whom she wanted, including Louis Armstrong and Basie, kept her brother Herschel, and recalls Lil Creole refusing to play.

segments.title: Recording with Sidney Bechet and Clarence Williams
segments.summary: She recalls the 1924 sessions with Clarence Williams and Bechet, "Off and On Blues" and records later sent by Williams's son.

segments.title: Okeh songs handed to her at sessions; "Mourning Dove Blues"
segments.summary: She sang songs given her at the Okeh office without practice and discusses 1925 sessions with Joe Oliver and Herschel and which tunes she wrote.

segments.title: Reading music and knowing her key
segments.summary: She says she can read music but prefers harmony and knowing her key, and can play any song in any key.

segments.title: Wrong sideman credit and tunes taken by others
segments.summary: A record lists a cornetist she never knew; she says others recorded her tunes and nothing could be done about it.

segments.title: "After My Laughter Came Tears" and the man she lived with after her husband
segments.summary: She sings a song that fits her life and talks about her husband's death and a long relationship with another Buddy, who died of a heart attack.

segments.title: Leaving Chicago for Detroit and stopping recording
segments.summary: She moved to Detroit in 1929 at her husband's brother's urging, hated recording, and the companies lost track of her; she played cabarets with a five-piece band.

segments.title: Recording again in 1945 with Albert Ammons
segments.summary: She was called back to Chicago in 1945 for "Bedroom Blues" and "Buzz Me" with Albert Ammons, who she says learned from Herschel.

segments.title: Detroit records for Clarence Blair's Fine Art label
segments.summary: She recalls 1959 and 1962 Detroit records for Clarence Blair, who co-wrote her songs, and a trio he had her hire.

segments.title: What the blues means to her; "Adam and Eve Had the Blues"
segments.summary: Wallace says the blues is anything miserable, mentions songs written with her brother, and plays a song she completed herself.

segments.title: Who counts as a classic blues singer
segments.summary: Asked what classic blues means, she names a few women she considers classic singers and calls Bessie Smith a barrelhouse singer.

segments.title: Why women sang the blues more than men; B.B. King
segments.summary: She says women feel the blues harder than men, who turn to gambling and drink, and that men are returning to the blues.

segments.title: Texas Nightingale and Illinois Songbird nicknames
segments.summary: She explains how newspapers and Okeh gave her the names Texas Nightingale and Illinois Songbird.

segments.title: "Sex in the Hand Blues" and Okeh's song supply
segments.summary: She recalls the 1925 tune for Buddy Christian and how songs were handed to her at the New York Okeh office.

segments.title: The Depression and World War II in Detroit
segments.summary: She says she did not suffer in the Depression because she kept working cabarets and clubs, and denies working as a nurse in the war.

segments.chapter: Second day: early memories, London 1966 and other singers
segments.title: Second day: tape header, April 15, 1979
segments.summary: Header for cassette sides 3-4.

segments.chapter: Second day: early memories, London 1966 and other singers
segments.title: Childhood stay in New Orleans
segments.summary: As a small child she stayed briefly in New Orleans with her brother, while her mother tried to keep him from the war.

segments.chapter: Second day: early memories, London 1966 and other singers
segments.title: Learning organ and piano at home
segments.summary: She learned on the organ her mother had at home, later got a piano, and taught herself with her brother George helping.

segments.chapter: Second day: early memories, London 1966 and other singers
segments.title: Victoria Spivey finds her for the London blues festival
segments.summary: Spivey and Lenny Kunstadt locate her in Detroit; Willie Dixon arranges the trip to London after her boyfriend Buddy objects.

segments.chapter: Second day: early memories, London 1966 and other singers
segments.title: Triumph in London and writing "Woman, Be Wise"
segments.summary: She was scared but drew huge crowds, and wrote "Woman, Be Wise" on the spot when the show wanted new songs.

segments.title: "A Man for Every Day" versus "Mighty Tight Woman"
segments.summary: Reitz points to the contrast between two of her songs; Wallace says each came in a different year and mood.

segments.title: What "I'm a Mighty Tight Woman" means
segments.summary: She explains the title as being tight in everything she does and devoted to a man.

segments.title: Ma Rainey in Chicago, her gold pieces and young lovers
segments.summary: She knew Ma Rainey, saw her robbed of her gold-piece necklace at her brother's house, and says Ma took young lovers.

segments.title: Her age, arthritis and feeling 16
segments.summary: She jokes about boyfriends and her children, mentions arthritis and a cane, and says being active keeps her feeling sixteen at eighty.

segments.title: Sarah Martin as a sister; her sister in Baltimore; her teeth
segments.summary: She calls Sarah Martin her sister, mentions a sister who is a doctor in Baltimore, and talks about her sore gums.

segments.title: Never going to New York to sing; Buddy held her back; Spivey's record company
segments.summary: She says Buddy would not let her pursue a New York career, that he was mean to her, and compares Spivey, who had Lenny Kunstadt behind her.

segments.title: Lucille Hegeman and Alberta Hunter on television
segments.summary: She briefly places Lucille Hegeman and enjoys seeing Alberta Hunter honored on television.

segments.title: Women singers' styles shifting toward stage and ballads
segments.summary: The interviewers ask whether she saw herself as different from Ethel Waters and Alberta Hunter; she says she kept her church sound and did not change style.

segments.title: Alberta Hunter, Ethel Waters, Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan and Pearl Bailey
segments.summary: She did not know Hunter or Waters personally, recalls Ella Fitzgerald's sister from the hospital, and likes Pearl Bailey.

segments.title: The Okeh Artists Ball, February 1926: what she sang
segments.summary: She remembers the big Okeh night, singing "Shorty George" and "Up the Country" with Herschel on piano, and the Wickman Sisters' show.

segments.title: Who played at the Okeh ball and the party afterward
segments.summary: She lists performers present, says it lasted until two in the morning with more white than Black guests, and why she could not enjoy it.

segments.title: Travelling in the 1920s with a private berth
segments.summary: She describes touring by train from New York with a private berth and maid, including a trip to California.

segments.title: The T.O.B.A. circuit: four or five shows a day
segments.summary: She says T.O.B.A. time in Texas and Louisiana was slavery for the number of shows, though rooming houses and treatment were fine, and trains were segregated.

segments.title: Pay as chorus girl, ballad singer and blues singer
segments.summary: She earned about $10.50 a week as a chorus girl and $13 as a ballad singer, and says she only learned to sing the blues when records came out.

segments.title: "I Feel Good" and closing the day
segments.summary: She says her brother George wrote "I Feel Good", sings it, and the session ends.

segments.title: Joe Oliver's house, his sponsoring her trips, his death and "Caldonia"
segments.summary: She visited Oliver's home in Chicago, he handled her songs and advised on her fee, and she says he died of ptomaine poisoning from sardines, costing her money for "Caldonia".

segments.title: Playing piano in a Detroit good-time house
segments.summary: After her mother died she played piano for room and board at a Detroit house run by a woman from Houston, before she went to Chicago.

segments.title: Naming her first songs and the session with Eddie Heywood
segments.summary: George urged her to name her songs, she called the first "Shorty George", and Eddie Haywood played the first session rather than George, adding his own tune.

segments.title: Joe Oliver as a gentleman
segments.summary: She remembers Joe Oliver as easy to get along with and gentle with a young girl.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong at the sessions and "Special Delivery Blues"
segments.summary: She recalls being buddies with Louis, who had a jealous wife, and how he joined "Special Delivery Blues" while her husband Matt was nervous.

segments.title: Lil Hardin and the origin of "I'm a Mighty Tight Woman"
segments.summary: Lil would not commit to playing her new song, so Wallace played it herself on record; Herschel played at the Okeh night.

segments.title: Who wrote the March 1926 session songs; Herschel's endings
segments.summary: She sorts out which songs were hers and which Clarence Blair's, how Louis played behind any song, and how Herschel's ending became "Mighty Tight Woman".

segments.title: Writing songs from her own feelings
segments.summary: She says every song she wrote came from her feelings and that she is only talking about herself.

segments.title: Working with Louis Armstrong, Jelly Roll Morton and Bennie Moten
segments.summary: She liked working with everyone, remembers Jelly Roll as older and distant, and says she sang with Bennie Moten's band.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Bonnie Raitt and the Butter Beans and Susie song
segments.summary: Wallace sings a line from a Susie song she does with Bonnie Raitt and talks about why Butter Beans and Susie were a hit and how Susie died.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Asked to sing "Jelly Roll Blues" in a Detroit church
segments.summary: A Methodist church on Woodward Avenue asked her to sing "Jelly Roll Blues"; she went through a storm and gave people what they wanted.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Bertha Chippie Hill and Johnny Dodds
segments.summary: She recalls Chippie Hill at the Okeh night, a dance called the Mess-Around, and Hill singing her "Shorty George Blues".

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Going to New York to record, six-month stays
segments.summary: She went to New York to record in 1924 and 1925, staying six or seven months each time though her brother objected.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Fats Waller, Clarence Williams and Eva Taylor
segments.summary: She went out often with Fats Waller, Clarence Williams was cautious, and she felt sorry for Eva Taylor under Williams's meanness.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Rent parties and chitlin' struts
segments.summary: She went to rent parties with Fats and midnight dinners at Clarence's, and compares New York and Chicago house parties.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Held up in a Harlem elevator
segments.summary: She tells of two men holding up her building's elevator on 141st Street while she was recording for Okeh, and the caretaker's police whistle.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Record pay, spending and clothes in the 1920s
segments.summary: She was paid about a hundred dollars a record, supported her brother and husband's mother, and saved nothing.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Cooking for herself in New York
segments.summary: She cooked steak, rice, greens and cornbread wherever she had a stove.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Third tape header, cassette sides 5-6
segments.summary: Header for cassette sides 5-6.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Living in New York: friends, bridge and the Nest
segments.summary: She stayed six months at a time in New York, played bridge with girlfriends, and went to the Nest for afternoon cabaret.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: How a recording session worked at Okeh
segments.summary: She describes rehearsing, timing, making two takes and the wax on the studio floor, taking two to three hours.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Rehearsing and travelling to the Okeh studio
segments.summary: She rehearsed at her pianist's room, including with Clarence Williams, and rode the el to the studio on 45th Street.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: Room rent and cooking a duck
segments.summary: She paid five or six dollars a week for a sleeping room and tells of ruining a duck by buttering it.

segments.chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
segments.title: New York versus Chicago
segments.summary: She liked New York but preferred Chicago because she knew more people there.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet
segments.summary: She loved Bechet's sax, always asked for him on records, and says her brother kept men from speaking to her.

segments.title: Victoria Spivey and Bessie Smith: cussing and drinking
segments.summary: She says Spivey was a mean woman who cussed and drank, and contrasts Bessie Smith's way of taking over a party.

segments.title: Writing "Flat Blues" after Bessie Smith's "Backwater Blues"
segments.summary: Okeh wanted a flood blues after Bessie's hit, so she wrote one in 1927 and explains the three-minute record limit.

segments.title: Why she became a blues singer and her heavy voice
segments.summary: Blues singers earned more, and she says her voice grew heavy after she got wet, which suited the blues.

segments.title: "Baby, I Can't Use You No More" and "Jealous Woman Like Me"
segments.summary: She explains songs she wrote when angry at her husband Matt and jealous over a woman named Stella.

segments.title: Writing songs as relief
segments.summary: She says writing the songs gave relief and told the truth about herself, including "A Man for Every Day in the Week".

segments.title: Niece Hocile's records and how alike they sang
segments.summary: They sorted out records credited to her but sung by Hocile, who was raised with her and died around 1940.

segments.title: Hocile's life in California and her children
segments.summary: Hocile lived in California, sang in a cabaret, had many children, and Sippie raised some after her death.

segments.title: Who played on Hocile's records
segments.summary: They correct the personnel on Hocile's recordings, with Herschel and Buddy Christian.

segments.title: Singing the blues to feel better
segments.summary: Wallace says she cries over her brother and Hocile, plans new blues, and says singing the blues eases her mind.

segments.title: "Trouble Everywhere I Go" and "Murder's Going to Be My Crime"
segments.summary: She explains the Houston good-time house behind one song and the jealous meaning of another.

segments.title: The 1966 Copenhagen record
segments.summary: She played piano on "Mighty Tight Woman" on a Copenhagen record, with Little Brother playing on the rest.

segments.title: How Spivey and Lenny Kunstadt found her for London
segments.summary: They called Willie Dixon from her house in Detroit to say they had found her, and she hesitated to go alone.

segments.title: Willie Dixon's audition and meeting Little Brother
segments.summary: She auditioned for Dixon, paid her own fare to Chicago, met Little Brother and the other musicians, and decided to go to London.

segments.title: The European tour and the Paris hold-up
segments.summary: The tour went from London to Paris, Geneva and Switzerland; robbers held up the Paris show but the receipts were recovered.

segments.title: Recording in Copenhagen with Little Brother
segments.summary: She recorded for two days' pay of $300 with Little Brother playing; she had taught him "Mighty Tight Woman".

segments.title: Her horoscope and Buddy's death
segments.summary: She says she watches her horoscope daily, more since Buddy died five years ago.

segments.title: Writing "You Got to Know How"
segments.summary: She says she wrote the song around the time of London, perhaps in Boston, and never sang it there.

segments.title: Singing risque lyrics then and now
segments.summary: She says she did not sing things like that in the 1920s, though Susie did, and "Mighty Tight Woman" got many requests in London.

segments.title: Writing "Woman, Be Wise" with a verse from Bonnie
segments.summary: She explains how "Woman, Be Wise" came about and that Bonnie wrote one verse.

segments.title: Being freer and lonelier in later life; jealous men
segments.summary: She enjoys life more now with no one to hold her down, but is lonely, and says men are jealous.

segments.title: Thinking of herself as a singer; talent in the family
segments.summary: She always thought of herself as a singer, taught by teachers and a cousin, and says musical talent is natural in her family.

segments.title: Artist versus celebrity; the award and church piano
segments.summary: She knew she was an artist but not a celebrity until a city award; she plays piano for a synagogue and a church.

segments.title: Handling money; the $5,000 first check
segments.summary: She gave money to her husband and brother, got $5,000 for "Shorty George" and "Up the Country", and fought to get her share from her brother.

segments.title: Living well in Chicago in the 1920s
segments.summary: Her brother set her up in a Chicago house with rooms for Herschel and family, and Ma Rainey and Susie visited.

segments.title: Ma Rainey robbed of her gold pieces again
segments.summary: She retells Ma Rainey being robbed and her brother stammering to her, placing it when she was not yet twenty.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong's role on her records and rehearsals
segments.summary: She says Louis followed her on the records, played only between songs, and did not need to rehearse every day.

segments.title: Cassette side 7 header
segments.summary: Header for cassette side 7.

segments.title: Wallace's closing remarks on Rosetta Reitz's visit
segments.summary: Wallace thanks Reitz for the visit, praises Little Brother and her pianist Dave, and says she keeps writing blues.

segments.title: Blues and gospel notebook; the church
segments.summary: She shows her blues and gospel notebook and says the only difference between them is the words.

segments.title: "Bedroom Blues" and loneliness
segments.summary: She talks about writing "Bedroom Blues" after her husband died, her loneliness and the costs of living alone.

segments.title: Her brother George's fall and death in Chicago
segments.summary: She tells how George broke his spine in a fall during a house fire and died in the hospital.

segments.title: Identifying and burying George; her faith after the loss
segments.summary: She and a cousin identified him at the morgue, buried him cheaply, and she says the Lord stood by her.

segments.title: Why singing the blues does not condemn her
segments.summary: Citing the Bible, she says God gave her talent and she feels no condemnation for singing the blues.

segments.title: Whether white people can feel the blues; television
segments.summary: She says some white people feel the blues but few would take what she took, then talks about her TV viewing.

segments.title: Prejudice now versus the 1920s
segments.summary: She thinks race relations are better, including seating on streetcars.
